abstract: Astrocyte-neuron interactions coordinate cholesterol metabolism, cell adhesion, and synaptic gene expression1,2, and related gene expression programs decline together in schizophrenia3. Whether pharmacological or genetic perturbations can selectively engage components of this coordinated biology was unknown. Here we combine genetically diverse cultures of human stem-cell-derived neurons and astrocytes, pharmacological profiling, genetic association mapping and CRISPR interference to examine these biological programs. In stem-cell-derived astrocyte mono-cultures, the antipsychotic clozapine induced a focused transcriptional response involving cholesterol biosynthesis and export, and drove an increase in intracellular and secreted cholesterol. This response overlapped with the cholesterol-related component of the astrocytic response to neuronal contact seen in neuron-astrocyte co-cultures, but did not extend to synaptic cell-adhesion genes. In neuron-astrocyte co-cultures, clozapine also increased neuronal firing. Across individual cell donors, cholesterol-pathway induction by clozapine was broadly shared but varied in magnitude. Gene-expression patterns in untreated donors were associated with differential responses to clozapine and the liver X receptor agonist GW3965. Common genetic variation influenced expression of several cholesterol-related genes, including a clozapine-dependent association of HSD17B7 expression with nearby genetic variants. Independently, repression of LDLR induced coordinated expression of cholesterol-biosynthesis genes in astrocytes that overlapped with astrocyte responses to clozapine and neuronal contact. These findings identify shared cholesterol-related transcriptional responses to pharmacological and genetic perturbations and link common genetic variation to distinct features of cholesterol-pathway responses.
